citation: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock and Mellers (2025), Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities, arXiv 2506.01578 v1 (PDF read in full)
text_source: 100 binary ForecastBench questions (2024-12-08 set) resolving December 2024; FRED, Yahoo Finance, Metaculus, Polymarket and others; no documents
feature: Probability under 37 single-element prompts (Study 1) and 17 compound, vendor-generated and literature prompts (Study 2) against one minimal control
method: Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B at temperature 0; o1 and o1-mini in Study 2; pre-registered mixed model on per-item Brier differences with Benjamini-Hochberg correction; t-tests as secondary
pit_handling: Vendor-stated cutoffs (Oct 2023 to Jul 2024) all before resolution; no between-model comparison
informs_decision: Expected playbook gain: best single prompts -0.011 to -0.019 Brier, not robust; compound prompts no better (best -0.009, n.s.); Bayesian updating +0.030, propose-evaluate-select +0.033, expert odds-ratio protocol +0.023 (all worse); persona n.s.; base-rate prompts the only consistent small gain; reasoning models same pattern

citation: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han and Steinhardt (2024), Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models, arXiv 2402.18563 v1 (HTML read)
text_source: 5,516 binary questions from Metaculus, GJOpen, INFER, Polymarket, Manifold (914 test, opened after cutoff); date-filtered news retrieval
feature: Probability from a retrieval-augmented system with a scratchpad prompt chosen from 15, a fine-tuned reasoner and a trimmed-mean ensemble
method: GPT-4-1106-Preview base and fine-tuned GPT-4-0613; prompt and hyperparameters chosen on validation; ablations removing fine-tuning and retrieval; five ensembling rules compared
outcome: Brier score; accuracy; RMS calibration error
horizon: Platform question horizons, five retrieval dates each
incremental_to: Human crowd (0.149); zero-shot and scratchpad baselines of 14 models
pit_handling: Test questions open after stated cutoff; train and validation resolved before; retrieval date-filtered; manual post-training leakage probe
informs_decision: Prompt structure alone is worth about 0.002 Brier (0.206 v 0.208 zero-shot); scratchpad no better than zero-shot without retrieval (GPT-4 0.209 v 0.208); averaging 6 samples -0.003, LLM aggregator +0.0015; system hedges and rarely gives low probabilities; select prompts on validation, test later in time

citation: Pratt, Blumberg, Kreitlon Carolino and Morris (2024), Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?, arXiv 2406.04446 v1 (HTML read)
text_source: GleanGen internal prediction market (Google); 351 validation and 341 test events; 78 open on 1 August 2022
feature: Probability under human forecasting strategies (breakdown, base rates, both sides, persona crowd, news) chained as LLM modules
method: PaLM 2 (pre-training ended July 2022); Brier, class-weighted Brier; with and without rationale; reversed-event coherence probe
horizon: From 1 August 2022 to resolution (many end of 2022)
incremental_to: Basic one-prompt baseline; human market midpoint
pit_handling: Model with known pre-training end; forecast date set just after it
informs_decision: No strategy beat the basic prompt (0.1221; breakdown 0.1895, base rates 0.1562); asking for a rationale raised probabilities across events; P(event) + P(not event) well below 1; check base rate and level shifts, not Brier alone

citation: Turpin, Michael, Perez and Bowman (2023), Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting, NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2305.04388 v2 (HTML read)
text_source: BIG-Bench Hard (13 tasks, 3,299 examples); BBQ (2,592 questions with weak evidence)
feature: Answer and chain-of-thought explanation under injected biasing features (suggested answer; answer always A; stereotypes)
method: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0; chain of thought v direct; zero-shot v few-shot; paired accuracy differences; hand annotation of explanations
outcome: Accuracy drop biased v unbiased; share of unfaithful pairs explained by stereotype
incremental_to: Same inputs without the biasing feature; no chain of thought
pit_handling: Not addressed (the biasing feature plays the role of a remembered outcome)
informs_decision: Hidden influences move answers by up to 36.3 points while explanations never mention them (1 of 426); 73% of unfaithful explanations argue for the biased answer; zero-shot reasoning can amplify the bias (39.5 to 23.3%); matches EXP-0029: stated reasons cannot audit the S2 call

citation: Lanham, Chen, Radhakrishnan and 27 others (2023), Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning, arXiv 2307.13702 v1 (HTML read)
text_source: Eight multiple-choice tasks (AQuA, LogiQA, MMLU, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, OpenBookQA, ARC Challenge and Easy)
feature: Dependence of the answer on the reasoning: early answering, added mistakes, filler tokens, paraphrase; by model size
method: 175B RLHF dialogue model, 100 sampled reasonings per question; Ganguli et al. size series for scaling
outcome: Share of answers unchanged after intervention (AOC); accuracy with v without reasoning
informs_decision: Reasoning is often post-hoc (early-answering AOC 0.02 to 0.44 by task); dependence unrelated to accuracy gain; larger models less faithful on 7 of 8 tasks; gives the truncation and edit tests for checking whether S2 probabilities depend on playbook output

citation: Sprague, Yin, Rodriguez and seven others (2025), To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning, ICLR 2025, arXiv 2409.12183 v3 (HTML read)
text_source: Meta-analysis of 110 papers (1,218 comparisons); own runs on 20 datasets with 14 models
feature: Accuracy of chain of thought v direct answer by task type; planning v execution v tool solver
method: Zero- and few-shot prompting, greedy decoding; paired bootstrap with Bonferroni; MMLU split by presence of '='; Python and Z3 solvers
pit_handling: GSM8K-Hard used against contamination; otherwise not addressed
informs_decision: Chain of thought helps math and symbolic tasks (+14.2, +12.3, +6.9 points) and little elsewhere (56.8 v 56.1); tools beat chain of thought at execution; so compute S2 arithmetic in code and expect little from free-text reasoning on judgement items; compare at matched compute

citation: Kim, Muhn and Nikolaev (2024), Financial Statement Analysis with Large Language Models, arXiv 2407.17866 v2 (HTML read for the prompt ablation only); withdrawn by the authors in v3
text_source: Standardised, anonymised Compustat statements; analyst sample and full sample 1968-2021
feature: Direction of next-year earnings from GPT-4 Turbo with a simple prompt v an analyst-style chain-of-thought prompt (trends, ratios with formulae, interpretation, prediction)
method: Same model and inputs, two prompts
pit_handling: Firm and year guessing near zero; withdrawn for data and analysis inconsistencies; Levy (2026, stream 08) attributes this kind of accuracy to recall
informs_decision: Analyst-step CoT 60.35% v simple prompt 52.33% (+8 points) is the most-cited finance case for an analyst playbook and carries no weight: withdrawn, not reproduced by Li et al. (2024), and consistent with CoT amplifying recall (EXP-0029)

citation: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park and Tetlock (2024), Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy, arXiv 2402.19379 v6 (abstract read; Science Advances 10(45) per the reference list of Schoenegger et al. 2025)
text_source: 31 binary questions from a three-month tournament with 925 human forecasters
feature: Aggregate of twelve LLMs' probabilities; GPT-4 and Claude 2 updating on the human median
method: Pre-registered comparison with the human crowd; equivalence tests
pit_handling: Questions resolved after the forecasts (live tournament)
informs_decision: Aggregating many models matched the human crowd; models showed an acquiescence bias (mean forecast above 50% with balanced outcomes); seeing the human median improved accuracy 17% to 28%; supports averaging over samples or models

citation: Tian, Mitchell, Zhou, Sharma, Rafailov, Yao, Finn and Manning (2023), Just Ask for Calibration, EMNLP 2023, arXiv 2305.14975 v2 (abstract read)
text_source: TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA
feature: Verbalised confidence v token probabilities of RLHF models
method: ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude; several elicitation prompts
informs_decision: Verbalised probabilities are often better calibrated than token probabilities (ECE down about 50% relative); supports asking the PM for a stated number

citation: Xiong, Hu, Lu, Li, Fu, He and Hooi (2024), Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2306.13063 v2 (abstract read)
text_source: Five dataset types (commonsense, arithmetic and others)
feature: Verbalised confidence under prompting, sampling and aggregation strategies
method: Five LLMs including GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat; calibration and failure prediction
informs_decision: Verbalised confidence is overconfident; consistency across multiple sampled answers and better aggregation reduce overconfidence; no method dominates; professional-knowledge tasks remain hard

citation: Fu, Conde, Martínez, Grandury and Reviriego (2026), Multiple Choice Questions: Reasoning Makes Large Language Models (LLMs) More Self-Confident, Especially When They are Wrong, IEEE Intelligent Systems 2026, arXiv 2501.09775 v3 (abstract of v3 and HTML of v2 read)
text_source: MMLU, 57 subjects
feature: Probability of the chosen option with direct answer v reasoning first
method: Seven LLMs; token probabilities; ECE and Brier
informs_decision: Reasoning first raises confidence for every model, more when the answer is wrong, and degrades calibration; with Pratt (2024), expect a reasons-first playbook to push S2 probabilities outward

citation: Kanishka and Mandora (2026), Structure Tax: How Structured Output affects LLMs Performance, AACL-IJCNLP 2026 (long), pages 4620-4644 (PDF read, sections 1 to 5)
text_source: GSM8K, MMLU, LogicBench, Spider
feature: Accuracy and calibration under JSON or XML outputs with the reasoning field before or after the answer field, against free form
method: GPT-4o, Gemini Flash 2.0, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 4B; temperature 0; five runs; prompt-perturbation robustness
informs_decision: Reasoning-first fields match or beat free form; answer-first collapses multi-step arithmetic (GSM8K: small models 10.98% v 83% to 87%; the reasoning-first lead was at least 37 points in every perturbation cell, GPT-4o included); XML beat JSON by up to 12.2 points; reasoning-first XML lowered ECE against free text for most models; a structured form is safe if reasoning precedes each answer, and answer-first is risky wherever the model must compute

citation: Chiang and Lee (2023), A Closer Look into Automatic Evaluation Using Large Language Models, Findings of EMNLP 2023, arXiv 2310.05657 v1 (PDF read, section 3)
text_source: SummEval and Topical-Chat meta-evaluation sets
feature: Correlation of ChatGPT ratings with human ratings under score only, rate-explain (rating then explanation) and analyze-rate (analysis then rating)
method: ChatGPT; G-Eval auto chain of thought compared; temperatures 0.3 and 0.7; prompt variants
outcome: Pearson and Kendall correlation with human ratings
informs_decision: Asking for an explanation after the rating helped as much as analysis before it; the rating cannot depend on the later text, so knowing an explanation is due changed the rating; supports a probability-first, reasons-after arm for judgement items

citation: Chen, Benton, Radhakrishnan and twelve others (2025), Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think, arXiv 2505.05410 v1 (abstract and HTML sections 1 to 3 read)
text_source: Prompts with six kinds of embedded hints
feature: Whether reasoning models verbalise hints they use
method: Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek R1 against Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) and DeepSeek V3; MMLU and GPQA prompt pairs with and without a hint; temperature 0; outcome-based RL experiments
informs_decision: Reasoning models verbalise hints they use in 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39% (DeepSeek R1) of cases; unfaithful traces are longer than faithful ones; RL raises faithfulness then plateaus; a frontier model's reasoning cannot rule out use of remembered outcomes, and length is no sign of honesty

citation: Arcuschin, Janiak, Krzyzanowski, Rajamanoharan, Nanda and Conmy (2026), Chain-of-Thought Reasoning In The Wild Is Not Always Faithful, ICML 2026, arXiv 2503.08679 v6 (abstract read)
text_source: Naturally worded paired comparative questions; hard math problems
feature: Implicit post-hoc rationalisation (Yes to both or No to both of a reversed pair) and illogical shortcuts
method: Production and thinking models
outcome: Rate of contradictory pairs justified by coherent reasoning
informs_decision: Rationalisation of an implicit bias occurs without any injected bias, up to 13% in production models and 0.04% to 0.37% in thinking models; reversed-question pairs are a cheap detector (same idea as the S2 coherence probe)

citation: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo and Griffiths (2025), Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse, arXiv 2410.21333 v4 (abstract read)
text_source: Six tasks from psychology where deliberation hurts humans
feature: Accuracy with and without chain of thought
method: State-of-the-art models including o1-preview and GPT-4o
informs_decision: Chain of thought cut accuracy by up to 36.3 points on three of six tasks; reasoning is not a safe default for pattern-like judgements

citation: Vamvourellis and Mehta (2025), Reasoning or Overthinking: Evaluating Large Language Models on Financial Sentiment Analysis, arXiv 2506.04574 v1 (abstract read)
text_source: Financial PhraseBank
feature: Zero-shot sentiment under fast (direct) and slow (chain of thought) prompting and reasoning models
method: GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, o3-mini; FinBERT baselines
outcome: Accuracy and agreement with expert labels
pit_handling: Not addressed (PhraseBank is old and public)
informs_decision: Best result was GPT-4o without chain of thought; reasoning did not help on a financial text judgement; weak finance evidence against reasons-first by default

citation: Nitarach, Sirichotedumrong, Pitchayarthorn, Taveekitworachai, Manakul and Pipatanakul (2025), FinCoT: Grounding Chain-of-Thought in Expert Financial Reasoning, FinNLP 2025 at EMNLP, arXiv 2506.16123 v5 (abstract read)
text_source: CFA-style questions in ten financial domains
feature: Accuracy under standard prompting, free chain of thought, structured chain of thought and expert-blueprint structured chain of thought
method: Qwen3-8B-Base and Fin-R1 (7B)
informs_decision: An expert blueprint raised a small base model from 63.2% to 80.5% and a finance-tuned model from 65.7% to 75.7%, most for models without financial post-training; domain checklists help weak models on knowledge questions, a setting far from a frontier model forecasting

citation: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov and Suhr (2024), Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.11324 v2 (abstract read)
text_source: Few-shot classification and generation tasks
feature: Performance across meaning-preserving prompt formats (FormatSpread)
method: Open LLMs including LLaMA-2-13B
informs_decision: Formats alone moved accuracy by up to 76 points and format rankings correlate weakly across models; report the spread across paraphrases of the control as the noise floor before crediting a playbook

citation: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee and Jurgens (2024), When 'A Helpful Assistant' Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts Do Not Improve Performances of Large Language Models, Findings of EMNLP 2024, arXiv 2311.10054 v3 (abstract read)
text_source: 2,410 factual questions
feature: Accuracy under 162 personas in the system prompt
method: Four LLM families; persona search strategies
informs_decision: Personas do not improve accuracy and their effects look random; with Schoenegger et al. (2025), drop the analyst or superforecaster persona or hold it fixed across arms

citation: Cook, Rocktäschel, Foerster, Aumiller and Wang (2024), TICKing All the Boxes: Generated Checklists Improve LLM Evaluation and Generation, arXiv 2410.03608 v1 (abstract read)
text_source: Instruction-following evaluations; LiveBench; WildBench
feature: LLM judgements structured by instruction-specific yes/no checklists
method: LLM-generated checklists; self-refinement and best-of-N with checklists
outcome: Exact agreement with human preferences; benchmark scores
informs_decision: Checklists raised judge-human exact agreement from 46.4% to 52.2% and human inter-annotator agreement from 0.194 to 0.256; checklists make judgements more consistent, which suits a separate reader filling a form more than the forecast itself

citation: Dhawka, Wilson and Head (2026), Programming Prescience: Issues in Human Construction of Forecasting Bots, arXiv 2611.12834 v1 (abstract read)
text_source: Interviews with 15 builders of forecasting bots from a recent AI forecasting competition
feature: How builders research, structure reasoning and evaluate bots
method: Qualitative interview study
informs_decision: Builders often added complexity that did not pay off and tested opportunistically and piecemeal; supports a fixed ablation plan and a ledger of every prompt version scored
